chapter: Records and playing in New Orleans
title: Real Dixieland, Raymond Burke and sitting in at Preservation Hall
summary: Julius says today's bands often depart from the real Dixieland his father taught, and describes a pianist praising his banjo at Preservation Hall.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: And the guy knew what they were doing. I mean, he could make plenty of noise, as I said. And so, he'd take right now. He'd take out here on Burden Street. I'm not criticizing.
But it's just, no, I can't. And it wouldn't make sense. But this is the thing I want to say. There's plenty real Dixaland. They're not playing out there.
Oh, that there's plenty of Dixaland that's not, they're not playing out there? That they're not playing, huh? I've heard this before.

I'm telling it like it is. Because I see lots of times. I go out there and I sit in with a band. I know the Dixaland number. And I see some guy look around at me. I say to myself, now you think I'm making the wrong card, but I'm playing it like it's supposed to be. You understand what I mean? But I had to jump back in with him to make things go along. Now, after the number stopped, Julius, I said, yes. I said, yes, I was wrong. He said, no, you wasn't wrong. He said, you were playing it like it's supposed to be. I said, well, yeah, y'all was cutting the number. I said, well, I had to cut off and go along the floor. Now, with these old 78's I have here, I have the Dukes of Dixaland. I have I don't know who and I don't know what all I don't have. I have Pat Swalers. That's the 40-year time. Shall we suggest to him what he can do with the 78's? Don't forget us. And so all those numbers. And then my daddy used to play all those Dixaland numbers, you understand? And hit me over the head with the bow when I make the wrong number. Well, I still think I'm going to hit if I make the wrong number, so I know when I'm out there. I started doing it like it's supposed to be dead, see? Or I had to cut him with the other guy, see? But it's hard, though. It's hard. When you know a number, you know, and someone cut it off, you have to... What exactly do you mean when you cut it off? What do they do? It's just like, uh, singing a number. You understand? It's like if you know the same part of it, and you start singing a number. You know what I'm saying? Why are you singing? See, like, I'm singing along with you. When it gets to a Satan part of it, I start singing the same a different way. You understand what I mean? Well, you're going to continue the way you know you write, but I'm wrong, see? Well, to keep me from being too wrong, you may drop over with me. You've got the shot cut. It's a shot cut. But it's, uh, I don't like it like that. If you're going to do something, do it just like it's supposed to be dead, and then... Because somebody's going to like it. Because if the real place of knowing it, it's not going to do you any good, because if the people that's hiring you to play it, if you don't tell you right then, one day, you may tell you that you didn't do it just like it. But you did. Because you can't fool everybody with music. You know what? You know what? At the preservation hall. A few weeks ago, they had a little party there. And, uh, I was invited. I went there. And we sit there, and we played, and, uh, no, the whole bunch was playing. I didn't bring my band band. They insisted on me bringing it. But I knew, uh, Claiborne's wife, she was going to have her band go. Because, uh, she's playing piano now. But she had her band go. So I went out there. And I took over from Batiste. And I just went on and did my thing. I wasn't thinking about anything else. I can't think of this fellow, elder fellow. He was playing piano. He told me, he says, uh, who are you? I said, I'm Julius. I said, I'm Julius. So, uh, someone say that's, uh, Captain John Handic's. I knew he had to be a hand.
What are you talking about? What was the name?
Planet player, uh, elder white fellow. I can't think of his name. Dave, do you know?

Well, I see. Raymond Burke? It could have been him. Luke Skiro? If you call his name, I couldn't call him. What did he look like? Luke Skiro. Luke Skiro. Did he have a mustache? Skiro, Skiro. Uh, yes. It's probably Raymond Burke. And so, he says, uh, Julius, I said, uh, he said, what's your name? I said, Julius Handic. You have to be a hand. He says, you was the honest banjo player. He said, that's just, he said, you make me play. I said, oh, go ahead. He said, yeah, you do. He said, you hold that time. He said, now I'm listening at you. I forget about the drums. He said, I'm listening at you. He said, you just pound him. He said, make me play. He said, you make me play. So the rest of the guys said, you're alright. So he said, Julius, he said, why don't you come out here? I said, well, And I thought I'd get a little straightened out. Well, the very time that I did say, well, I'm going out on Burden Street and get around. And then I don't think that I should go out there and I feel like resting myself because I'm into you. My name is in all the books. I have cards out there. And practically everybody knows me. If they want me, call me. I'll be there.
Oh, but so easy. You know, out of mind, out of sight, out of mind. That's awfully true.

Yes. And so, but behind, so much grief in between. You know what I mean? It just knocks the spirit out of me. Then when I get out there, it's going to come back anyway. So I say. When was the last time you played?
